keptItems.title: The Tension Between Two of the Democrats’ Biggest Promises
keptItems.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. On Wednesday morning, Americans awoke to the news that the Democrats had retaken both the House and the Senate. The next day, the stock market hemorrhaged $2.5 trillion. The tech sector was hardest hit. Alphabet, Nvidia, and the major semiconductor companies shed billions. Tesla and SpaceX, whose founder, Elon Musk, had spent half a billion dollars trying to keep Democrats out of Congress, were suddenly worth approximately $420 billion less than they had been two days before. In some ways, the election results were a referendum on Big Tech. Recent polls have revealed that most voters want the government to impose new regulations on AI, and many victorious Democrats campaigned on a promise to move away from the unchecked expansionism that has defined the industry during the Donald Trump era. Texas Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-Elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina have both pledged to stop the construction of new data centers, which have been the subject of voter panic across the country in recent months. (These facilities—physical manifestations of the industry’s clout—can raise local electricity costs and pollute the air.) Others vowed to stand up to imperious Silicon Valley elites, or to hold the president accountable for his corruption—much of which is linked to his family’s cryptocurrency ventures. keptItems.title: Prepare for the AI Apocalypse Like You’d Prepare for a Snowstorm
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Since late last year, a small but growing chorus of cybersecurity experts has been warning that AI models were pushing the internet toward a sort of cataclysm. Hospitals, banks, utilities, basically anything and everything connected to the web could be hacked. Over the past month or so, those scenarios have come alive in almost spectacular fashion: Last month, AI was used to find major security flaws in software used by 70 percent of websites, prompting governments to take down their websites as a precaution. A week later, attackers targeted the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, in part by hijacking the company’s internal AI tools, and ultimately drained billions of dollars. This fall alone, AI has been used to hack hundreds of financial institutions in Latin America, not to mention data centers, banks, and government entities around the world. AI has also changed the economics of hacking, such that targeting individual people and small organizations is becoming cheap and easy enough to be worthwhile. And there’s a broader rise in cyberattacks that, though not directly tied to AI, likely leveraged the technology in some way. Last week, for instance, the FBI issued a warning about hacks targeting industrial refrigeration systems following attacks on grocery stores in France, Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Israel, and other countries. keptItems.title: The Scapegals
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Susie Wiles should have been untouchable. She’d been with President Trump since his first bid for the White House. She was one of the few people who’d stuck around after the January 6 attacks on the U.S. Capitol, when just about everyone else thought his political career was over. And as his chief of staff for the past two years, she was a stabilizing force in an administration that sorely needed one. But Wiles—whom Trump jettisoned last week after Republicans’ devastating midterm losses—likely had at least one thing working against her: that second X chromosome. Since returning to the White House, Trump has refrained from the firing sprees of his first term, but he has shown a remarkable willingness to discard his female senior administration officials when they displease him. With the abrupt elevation of Stephen Miller to chief of staff last Friday, Wiles joined that most unenviable troop—The Scapegals. keptItems.title: Jensen Huang’s Apology May Be the Only Correct Use of AI
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Look, I just want to say that if Nvidia CEO and reported spy-plot target Jensen Huang did get help from AI to write an apology email to his family and company about his affair (he’s said he uses AI to help write all of his first drafts), this might be the one use of AI that makes sense to me. People (me) are always saying about AI, “This is a solution looking for a problem!” and “Who would possibly want to delegate things like knowing information about your children or creating works of art to a third-party series of zeroes and ones?” But there are some things in life that nobody wants to do, such as get a root canal, amputate a limb, or deal with your cable provider. Or, perhaps, apologize simultaneously to your employees and your wife of 40 years for jeopardizing your business and personal relationships and perhaps also national security? (To me, though, those feel like two separate emails.) But I do see one problem for someone attempting to delegate the writing of this email: I don’t think this specific email has ever been written before, by anyone. “Business/Personal Email Apologizing for Affair/Possible National-Security Breach” is the email equivalent of those wedding dress codes—“Beach Formal”; “Back-of-Your-Closet Country Club”; “Cocktail Business Black Tie”—that are beyond what the human brain can understand. I’m just wondering what training data set one would even consult in this scenario. What template was AI going to work with here? James Bond scripts? keptItems.title: Why Pete Hegseth Faces Impeachment
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Thomas Massie is pushing the House to impeach Pete Hegseth, the Cabinet member most closely associated with the Iran war. The representative from Kentucky’s argument is that if Republicans like him don’t hold the secretary of defense accountable now for his various abuses of power, Democrats will in January. A vote in the House could come as soon as this evening. Massie, who was ousted by a Trump-backed primary opponent earlier this year, introduced his articles of impeachment against the defense secretary yesterday. It is Massie’s second attempt, following an unsuccessful effort in September. That time around, House Speaker Mike Johnson sent lawmakers home for recess instead of allowing a vote. Senator Ted Cruz said yesterday on his podcast that Johnson’s move was in part motivated by the fact that Republicans “didn’t have the votes to stop a Hegseth impeachment.” This time could end differently: Although most Republicans are likely to close ranks behind the GOP defense secretary in the middle of a war, only a few defections would create a majority for impeachment. The eight articles in Massie’s impeachment resolution focus primarily on four issues: the Iran war, the Pentagon’s campaign of boat strikes, Hegseth’s attempt to punish lawmakers for warning service members not to follow illegal orders, and the military operation in January to capture the Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro. keptItems.title: Trump Has Been Corroded by Hate
keptItems.summaryEvidence: “L et’s talk about death .” That’s what the 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat said to President Trump near the end of their interview that aired Sunday. Douthat asked Trump what he thought would happen to him when he dies. “I’m a religious person, so in theory I go to heaven,” the president said. When Douthat pressed him on whether he actually believes he’s going to heaven, Trump replied, “I hope so. I don’t want to go to hell.” Douthat then posed a hypothetical: “Let’s say you pass away, you’re entering the next life, and all you have to do to enter paradise is feel love and forgiveness for James Comey, Nancy Pelosi, anyone who you have expressed hate for over the years. Do you think you can do it?” Trump acknowledged that the easy answer would be, Oh, yes, I could forgive . He didn’t give it. “I found them to be extremely dishonest people, very bad people, very bad for our country,” he said. Pressed again, he was blunt: “The answer is no.” “Before the judgment throne of God?” Douthat asked. Trump didn’t budge. “No, I think they were very bad people and—I dislike, I can use the word hate , I do hate some of my enemies.” Moments later, he removed any doubt. Even before the judgment throne of God, with his eternal salvation at stake, would he forgive his enemies? “No, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.” N O POLITICIAN IN AMERICAN HISTORY has told as many lies as Trump. But on this question, I believe he was telling the truth. In one respect I give him credit for it. He might have just said he could forgive. That’s the answer we’re taught to give. Jes
